keyVerseText: And they appointed two, Joseph called Barsabas, who was surnamed Justus, and Matthias.
rootMeaning: The name Ἰοῦστος (Ioûstos) is of Latin origin, derived from the word "just," which conveys the idea of righteousness, fairness, and moral integrity. This root meaning enriches the common English gloss "Justus" by emphasizing not only legal justice but also a character marked by uprightness and faithfulness. Although it is a proper noun, the name carries the weight of these ethical and spiritual qualities inherent in its etymology.
usageInScripture: The word Ἰοῦστος appears three times in the New Testament, always as a proper name translated "Justus." It identifies three different early Christians: Joseph Barsabbas (Acts 1:23), Titus of Corinth (Acts 18:7), and a Christian in Rome (Colossians 4:11). This consistent translation as a personal name highlights its function as an identifier of faithful believers rather than a descriptive term, yet its root meaning subtly underscores their reputations for righteousness within the early church.
theologicalSignificance: The name Justus, rooted in the concept of justice and righteousness, reminds believers that the Christian life is marked by moral integrity and faithfulness to God's standards. Each individual bearing this name in Scripture represents the reality that God calls His people to live justly in the world as a reflection of His own character. This underscores the evangelical truth that salvation is not only about forgiveness but also about transformation into Christlike holiness. Recognizing the meaning behind Ἰοῦστος encourages believers to pursue a life worthy of their calling, embodying justice as a testimony to the gospel.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 1:23 introduces Joseph called Barsabbas, surnamed Justus, chosen alongside Matthias to replace Judas as an apostle. The use of the name Justus here signals his reputation for righteousness and reliability, qualities essential for apostolic ministry. This highlights the early church's high standard for leadership, emphasizing that those who serve must be just in character, reflecting God's own justice. The name enriches the verse by portraying the spiritual integrity expected in those who carry forward Christ's mission.
